note: Candidate sources of the Landmark Ledger, drafted in the cloud from memory and partial search; nothing here is verified. Input for Kobol batch K2. Fields: candidates (the claim each source must support: title, first_published, one_line, who) and items (one row per cited URL: slug, role source or reaction, i the index, kind, url or null, title, claim the cloud draft says the page shows).

candidates.title: AI model disproves Erdős's unit distance conjecture
who: External checkers: Noga Alon, Thomas Bloom, Tim Gowers and six others
candidates.one_line: An OpenAI reasoning model built point sets in the plane with more than n^(1+d) unit-distance pairs for a fixed d above zero, disproving Erdős's 1946 conjecture. External mathematicians checked the proof.

candidates.title: Kakeya sets in three dimensions have full dimension
who: Joshua Zahl (University of British Columbia, from memory)
candidates.one_line: Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl proved that every Kakeya set in three-dimensional space, a set holding a unit line segment in every direction, has Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension 3.

candidates.title: Sphere packing solved in dimensions 8 and 24
who: Henry Cohn, Abhinav Kumar, Stephen D. Miller, Danylo Radchenko and Maryna Viazovska (dimension 24)
candidates.one_line: Viazovska proved the E8 lattice is the densest sphere packing in 8 dimensions. With four co-authors she proved the same for the Leech lattice in 24 dimensions, using modular forms.

candidates.title: Marton's conjecture on small doubling proved in characteristic 2
who: W. T. Gowers, Ben Green, Freddie Manners and Terence Tao
Lean formalisation team led by Tao with Yael Dillies, Bhavik Mehta and others
candidates.one_line: Gowers, Green, Manners and Tao proved Marton's conjecture in characteristic 2: a set with small doubling lies in few cosets of a small subspace. A Lean proof followed in about three weeks.

candidates.title: AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry 2 reach IMO silver-medal level
candidates.one_line: Google DeepMind's AlphaProof, which writes Lean proofs a computer can check, and AlphaGeometry 2 solved 4 of 6 problems at the 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad, scoring 28 of 42.

candidates.title: First exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey numbers since 1935
who: Marcelo Campos, Simon Griffiths, Robert Morris and Julian Sahasrabudhe
candidates.one_line: Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe proved that R(k), the least size forcing a one-colour clique of k points, is at most (4 minus e) to the k, the first exponential gain since 1935.

candidates.title: Hodge theory proves the Heron-Rota-Welsh conjecture for matroids
who: Karim Adiprasito, June Huh and Eric Katz
candidates.one_line: Adiprasito, Huh and Katz used Hodge theory to prove that the coefficients of a matroid's characteristic polynomial are log-concave, settling the Heron-Rota-Welsh conjecture.

candidates.title: AlphaEvolve finds 48-multiplication scheme for 4x4 complex matrices
candidates.one_line: DeepMind's AlphaEvolve found a way to multiply two 4x4 complex matrices with 48 scalar multiplications, and matched or beat the best known results on most of over 50 open problems it tried.

candidates.title: Lean finishes computer check of the liquid vector space theorem
who: Lean community team led by Johan Commelin
Peter Scholze and Dustin Clausen (original theorem)
candidates.one_line: A Lean community team led by Johan Commelin finished a computer-checked proof of the Clausen-Scholze theorem on liquid vector spaces, which Peter Scholze had asked to have formally checked.

candidates.title: AlphaTensor finds faster matrix multiplication schemes for some sizes
candidates.one_line: DeepMind's AlphaTensor, a reinforcement-learning system, found matrix multiplication schemes with fewer steps for some sizes, including 47 products for 4x4 matrices over two-element arithmetic, against 49 before.

candidates.title: GPT-5.4 Pro proves Erdős problem 1196 on primitive sets
who: Liam Price (prompter) with OpenAI's GPT-5.4 Pro
Write-up by Alexeev, Barreto, Li, Lichtman, Price, Shah, Tang and Tao
candidates.one_line: GPT-5.4 Pro, prompted by Liam Price, proved the Erdős, Sárközy and Szemerédi conjecture that, for large primitive sets, the sum of 1/(a log a) is at most 1 plus a vanishing term.

candidates.title: Sensitivity conjecture proved with a short matrix argument
candidates.one_line: Hao Huang proved that any set of more than half the corners of an n-dimensional cube contains a corner with at least root-n neighbours in the set, which settles Nisan and Szegedy's sensitivity conjecture.

candidates.title: Kelley and Meka's strong bounds for three-term progressions
candidates.one_line: Kelley and Meka showed that a set of integers up to N with density exp(minus (log N) to a small power) must contain a three-term arithmetic progression, far beyond earlier bounds.

candidates.title: AI completes Lean formalisation of sphere packing in dimensions 8 and 24
who: Sphere Packing Project maintainers (Hariharan, Birkbeck, Lee and others)
candidates.one_line: Math, Inc.'s AI system Gauss finished the Lean formalisation of Viazovska's sphere packing proofs, dimension 8 in about five days and dimension 24 in about two weeks, with project maintainers reviewing the code.

candidates.title: Gemini Deep Think reaches gold-medal level at the 2025 IMO
ai_systems: Gemini Deep Think, advanced version (Google DeepMind)
candidates.one_line: An advanced version of Gemini Deep Think solved five of six 2025 IMO problems in natural language within the time limit, scoring 35 of 42; IMO coordinators graded and certified the answers.

candidates.title: AI and Lean settle Erdős problem 728 on factorial divisibility
who: Kevin Barreto with OpenAI's GPT-5.2 Pro and Harmonic's Aristotle
candidates.one_line: Using GPT-5.2 Pro and Harmonic's Aristotle, Kevin Barreto proved a version of Erdős problem 728: infinitely many factorial divisibilities a! b! dividing n! (a+b-n)! with a+b-n near log n. Lean checked it.

candidates.title: Gravitational waves and light seen together from a neutron-star merger
who: LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration
Optical follow-up teams (Swope, Las Cumbres Observatory, ePESSTO and others)
candidates.one_line: LIGO and Virgo heard two neutron stars merge on 17 August 2017. Telescopes then saw the afterglow, a kilonova that forges heavy elements, in many independent observations.

candidates.title: Four pulsar timing teams report a background of gravitational waves
who: European Pulsar Timing Array with the Indian Pulsar Timing Array
candidates.one_line: Timing of radio pulsars over years found a low-frequency hum of gravitational waves, likely from pairs of giant black holes. Four separate arrays announced consistent evidence on the same day.

candidates.title: JWST spectra confirm very early galaxies at redshifts above 10
who: JADES Collaboration (Univ. of Hertfordshire, Univ. of Cambridge, Univ. of Arizona and others)
CEERS team (NSF NOIRLab, Univ. of Texas at Austin and others)
candidates.one_line: Spectra from the James Webb Space Telescope showed that galaxies seen in early images really sit at redshifts above 10, meaning they formed within about 500 million years of the Big Bang.

candidates.title: Twisted bilayer graphene turns superconducting at a magic angle
candidates.one_line: Two stacked graphene sheets twisted by about 1.1 degrees become insulators and, with doping, superconductors. Two other labs reproduced the effect, opening the field of twistronics.

candidates.title: Three teams close the loopholes in tests of Bell's theorem
who: National Institute of Standards and Technology (Boulder)
candidates.one_line: Experiments in Delft, Vienna and at NIST each showed, without the main escape routes, that nature violates local realism, as quantum theory predicts. The three results came within weeks.

candidates.title: Two teams entangle pairs of vibrating drumheads
who: National Institute of Standards and Technology, Boulder (Teufel group)
candidates.one_line: Two groups, using different methods, entangled the motion of micrometre-scale vibrating drumheads, objects made of trillions of atoms. Their papers appeared back to back in Science in 2021.

candidates.title: Fermilab confirms the muon's magnetic moment is above the Standard Model value
candidates.one_line: Fermilab measured how the muon wobbles in a magnetic field and agreed with Brookhaven's earlier measurement, together 4.2 sigma above the standard theory value. The size of the gap depends on which theory value is used.

candidates.title: Weyl fermions are observed for the first time in a crystal
who: Institute of Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (Ding and Weng, Fang groups)
candidates.one_line: Two groups found, in the crystal tantalum arsenide, electron states that behave as Weyl fermions, with the surface 'Fermi arcs' that theory predicts. Their work appeared within days of each other.

candidates.title: Three teams see ultracold fermion gases turn more transparent
who: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder (Ye group)
candidates.one_line: Cold clouds of fermionic atoms scatter less light because the Pauli exclusion principle blocks atoms from changing state. Three groups, two in the United States and one in New Zealand, saw the effect within days of each other.

candidates.title: LIGO detects gravitational waves from two merging black holes
who: LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration
candidates.one_line: Two Advanced LIGO detectors recorded the ripples from two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses merging 1.3 billion years ago, the first direct detection of gravitational waves.

candidates.title: First image of a black hole's shadow, in galaxy M87
candidates.one_line: Radio dishes across the world acted as one telescope and imaged a bright ring around the black hole at the centre of galaxy M87, with a dark shadow matching general relativity.

candidates.title: Hydrogen sulfide superconducts at 203 kelvin under very high pressure
who: Max Planck Institute for Chemistry, Mainz (Eremets group)
Jilin University (Cui group, independent magnetic evidence)
candidates.one_line: Squeezed to about 1.5 million atmospheres, hydrogen sulfide loses electrical resistance at minus 70 degrees Celsius, a record. A group at Jilin University later reported magnetic evidence of superconductivity in the same compound.

candidates.title: A spacecraft crash changes an asteroid's orbit for the first time
who: NASA and Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (DART team)
Ground-based observers outside the DART team
candidates.one_line: NASA's DART spacecraft hit the small moon Dimorphos on 26 September 2022 and shortened its orbit by about half an hour, measured by telescopes on Earth. It is the first test of planetary defence.

candidates.title: A neutral-atom processor runs error-corrected logical qubits, up to 48
who: Harvard University, MIT and QuEra Computing (Lukin group)
candidates.one_line: Arrays of laser-trapped atoms were rearranged to encode and process up to 48 logical qubits with error detection, and logical circuits beat their physical counterparts. Trapped-ion teams reported similar gains.

candidates.title: Lasers excite the thorium-229 nucleus, a step to a nuclear clock
who: PTB, TU Wien and LMU Munich (Tiedau et al.)
University of California, Los Angeles (Elwell et al.)
JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder (Zhang et al.)
candidates.one_line: Three groups used lasers to excite the unusually low-energy nuclear transition of thorium-229 in crystals, and one tied its frequency to an atomic clock, the first step toward a nuclear clock.

candidates.title: ATLAS and CMS observe quantum entanglement between top quarks
candidates.one_line: Both big LHC experiments measured spin correlations between top quarks and found entanglement, at the highest energy yet tested. The two collaborations work independently.

candidates.title: Google claims a quantum computer beat supercomputers at a sampling task
who: University of Science and Technology of China (Zuchongzhi repeat)
candidates.one_line: A 53-qubit chip sampled random circuits in minutes; Google estimated a supercomputer would need thousands of years. Classical algorithms later cut that gap sharply, and a Chinese chip repeated the task.

candidates.title: Google's Willow chip lowers quantum errors as the code grows
who: University of Science and Technology of China (Zuchongzhi repeat)
candidates.one_line: On a 105-qubit chip, bigger surface-code blocks of qubits made logical errors fall by about half at each step, passing the threshold that makes large-scale error correction possible.

candidates.title: Reinforcement learning controls plasma in a tokamak fusion device
ai_systems: DeepMind deep reinforcement learning plasma controller
candidates.one_line: A neural-network controller trained in simulation ran the magnetic coils of the TCV tokamak and shaped hot plasma into several forms, including two plasma columns at once.

candidates.title: NIF fusion shot yields more energy than the laser delivered
who: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, National Ignition Facility
candidates.one_line: On 5 December 2022 a laser shot at the NIF made about 3.15 megajoules of fusion energy from about 2.05 megajoules of laser light on target, the first fusion gain above one in a lab.

candidates.title: A neural network decodes quantum errors better than hand-built decoders
candidates.one_line: A transformer-based decoder, trained on simulated and real data from Google's Sycamore chip, read error signals from a surface code more accurately than the best human-designed decoders.

candidates.title: AI conjectures a formula that shows single-minus gluon amplitudes are nonzero
ai_systems: an internal scaffolded GPT-5.2 model at OpenAI
who: Institute for Advanced Study, Vanderbilt University, University of Cambridge and Harvard University (human authors)
candidates.one_line: Physicists showed that a gluon scattering amplitude long assumed zero is nonzero in a special setting. GPT-5.2 Pro simplified their hand results and conjectured the general formula, which an internal model then proved.

candidates.title: Three teams measure very high heat conduction in boron arsenide
who: University of California, Los Angeles (Yongjie Hu group)
University of Texas at Dallas with the University of Illinois (Bing Lv, David Cahill)
University of Houston with Boston College and MIT (Zhifeng Ren, David Broido, Gang Chen)
candidates.one_line: Three groups grew cubic boron arsenide crystals and each reported thermal conductivity near 1,000 watts per metre kelvin, close to a 2013 theory prediction and far above most metals.

candidates.title: An engineered enzyme breaks down PET plastic for recycling
candidates.one_line: An enzyme engineered from a compost enzyme broke down most of a batch of waste PET into its building blocks in about ten hours. A company then ran a demonstration plant and made new bottles from the output.

candidates.title: A neural-network program plans chemical syntheses that chemists rate as equal
ai_systems: 3N-MCTS (three neural networks with Monte Carlo tree search), University of Munster
who: University of Munster (Marwin Segler, Mike Preuss, Mark Waller)
candidates.one_line: A search program guided by neural networks, trained on millions of published reactions, planned routes to target molecules. In a double-blind test, chemists did not prefer published routes over its routes.

candidates.title: Deep learning predicts 2.2 million new stable crystal structures
ai_systems: GNoME (Graph Networks for Materials Exploration), Google DeepMind
candidates.one_line: Graph neural networks trained by active learning predicted 2.2 million crystal structures, about 381,000 of them on the updated stability hull. Critics asked how many are new, useful or realistic compounds.

candidates.title: An AI-guided robot lab reports making 41 new inorganic materials
ai_systems: A-Lab (machine-learning recipe and diffraction-analysis models with robotic stations), Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory
who: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and University of California, Berkeley (Gerbrand Ceder, Kristin Persson groups)
candidates.one_line: A robotic lab, with machine-learning models choosing recipes and reading X-ray patterns, tried 58 target compounds over 17 days and reported making 41. A later analysis questioned how many were new or correctly identified.

candidates.title: A mobile robot chemist found a more active photocatalyst on its own
ai_systems: Mobile robotic chemist with a Bayesian search algorithm, University of Liverpool
candidates.one_line: A free-roaming robot ran 688 experiments over eight days, using a search algorithm to pick each next step, and found a photocatalyst mixture about six times more active at making hydrogen from water.

candidates.title: A language-model agent planned and ran chemistry experiments on its own
ai_systems: Coscientist (an agent built on GPT-4 from OpenAI), Carnegie Mellon University
candidates.one_line: An agent built on a large language model read documentation, planned and ran palladium-coupling reactions in an automated lab, and tuned a reaction. The paper also tested how it handled requests for banned substances.

candidates.title: Software plans the synthesis of complex natural products, and chemists make them
who: Institute of Organic Chemistry, Polish Academy of Sciences
Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (IBS Center for Soft and Living Matter)
candidates.one_line: A computer program, using rules and search rather than learned patterns alone, planned routes to complex natural products. Chemists then ran the planned syntheses in the lab, with some changes made along the way.

candidates.title: A neural-network density functional handles fractional electrons better
candidates.one_line: DeepMind trained a neural network, DM21, as a density functional for electrons in molecules. It cut two systematic errors, fractional charge and fractional spin, that limit standard functionals in the tests reported.

candidates.title: Closed-loop machine learning picks better fast-charging plans for batteries
ai_systems: Bayesian optimisation with an early-outcome predictor, Stanford University, MIT and Toyota Research Institute
candidates.one_line: A machine-learning loop chose which fast-charging plans to test among 224 candidates, using early cycling data to predict lifetime. It found long-lived plans with far less testing time than a grid search would need.

candidates.title: Active machine learning finds a copper-aluminium catalyst for CO2 to ethylene
ai_systems: Active machine-learning screening of DFT data, University of Toronto and Carnegie Mellon University
candidates.one_line: A machine-learning loop searched calculated data for hundreds of copper-based materials and proposed copper-aluminium. Lab tests showed it turns CO2 into ethylene with about 80 percent efficiency at high current.

candidates.title: A generative AI model designs crystals; one was made in a lab
ai_systems: MatterGen (diffusion model for crystal structures), Microsoft Research
who: Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology (synthesis and measurement)
candidates.one_line: A diffusion model generated crystal structures for requested properties. For one design, a tantalum chromium oxide, collaborators made the material and measured a bulk modulus within 20 percent of the target.

candidates.title: Machine learning helps engineer an enzyme that breaks down PET plastic
ai_systems: MutCompute (3D neural network for choosing protein mutations), University of Texas at Austin
who: University of Texas at Austin (Hal Alper, Andrew Ellington groups)
candidates.one_line: A neural network suggested mutations to a PET-degrading enzyme. The engineered enzyme broke down many kinds of post-consumer PET at mild temperatures in the lab.

candidates.title: A metal-organic framework pulls drinking water from dry desert air
who: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Evelyn Wang group)
University of California, Berkeley (Omar Yaghi group)
candidates.one_line: A zirconium-based metal-organic framework took up water from air at low humidity and released it with sunlight-level heat. A later field test in a US desert collected drinking water without electricity.

candidates.title: Deep learning finds halicin, a new kind of antibiotic
ai_systems: Directed message-passing neural network, Broad Institute and MIT
who: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (James Collins and Regina Barzilay groups)
candidates.one_line: A neural network trained on growth data screened more than 100 million molecules and flagged halicin. It killed many drug-resistant bacteria in lab dishes and cleared infections in mice.

candidates.title: Chemists make and image a ring of 18 carbon atoms
candidates.one_line: Using an atomic-force microscope tip on a surface, the team stripped a precursor molecule down to cyclo[18]carbon and imaged a ring with alternating triple and single bonds.

candidates.title: AlphaFold 2 predicts protein structures at near-experimental accuracy in CASP14
candidates.one_line: In the blind CASP14 contest, DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 predicted the 3D shapes of proteins far more accurately than any other entry, often close to experimental structures.

candidates.title: AI-discovered drug rentosertib meets its safety goal in a phase 2a lung fibrosis trial
candidates.one_line: Rentosertib, found with generative AI for both its target and its molecule, met its safety goal in a phase 2a trial in lung fibrosis. Lung capacity rose on the drug and fell on placebo, an exploratory result in a small trial.

candidates.title: AI knowledge graph flags baricitinib for COVID-19, later approved by the FDA
candidates.one_line: In February 2020 an AI knowledge graph picked out baricitinib, an arthritis drug, as a possible COVID-19 treatment. Later trials by other teams backed it and the FDA approved it for hospitalised adults.

candidates.title: AI-supported mammography screening matches double reading with less workload
who: Lund University and Skane University Hospital
candidates.one_line: In Sweden's MASAI randomised trial, AI-supported mammogram reading found breast cancer as well as standard double reading and cut the number of screen readings radiologists had to do by close to half.

candidates.title: FDA permits marketing of first autonomous AI diagnostic, for diabetic retinopathy
candidates.one_line: The FDA allowed IDx-DR, software that reads retinal photos and decides on its own whether a patient has more than mild diabetic retinopathy, with no clinician reading the image.

candidates.title: mRNA COVID-19 vaccines prevent about 95 percent of cases in large trials
who: Moderna and the US National Institutes of Health
candidates.one_line: Phase 3 trials of two mRNA COVID-19 vaccines showed about 95 percent protection against symptomatic disease, and the FDA authorised the first on 11 December 2020.

candidates.title: First CRISPR gene-editing therapy for sickle cell disease reaches approval
candidates.one_line: Patients with sickle cell disease or beta-thalassaemia stopped needing transfusions or had no pain crises after their own blood stem cells were edited with CRISPR-Cas9. Casgevy was approved in late 2023.

candidates.title: Twice-yearly lenacapavir shots prevent HIV in a large trial of women
who: PURPOSE 1 investigators in South Africa and Uganda
candidates.one_line: In the PURPOSE 1 trial, no young women given lenacapavir injections twice a year acquired HIV, while infections occurred in women taking a daily pill. Regulators later approved it for prevention.

candidates.title: Weekly semaglutide lowers body weight by about 15 percent in trial
candidates.one_line: In the STEP 1 trial, adults with obesity who took weekly semaglutide lost on average about 15 percent of their body weight in 68 weeks, far more than on placebo. The FDA approved it as Wegovy.

candidates.title: Triple drug Trikafta treats the cause of cystic fibrosis for most patients
candidates.one_line: A combination of three drugs that help the faulty CFTR protein work gave large gains in lung function in two phase 3 trials, and the FDA approved it in October 2019 for most people with cystic fibrosis.

candidates.title: Ebola antibody drugs cut deaths in the PALM trial, then won approval
who: US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases
Institut National de Recherche Biomedicale (Democratic Republic of the Congo)
candidates.one_line: In a trial run during the Congo outbreak, two antibody treatments, REGN-EB3 and mAb114, gave much lower death rates than two other drugs. The FDA approved both in 2020.

candidates.title: Oral nirmatrelvir with ritonavir cuts COVID-19 hospital admission and death
candidates.one_line: The oral drug pair nirmatrelvir and ritonavir (Paxlovid) cut hospital admission or death among high-risk, unvaccinated adults with COVID-19 by close to 90 percent when given early. The FDA authorised it in 2021.

candidates.title: Lecanemab slows decline in early Alzheimer's disease in a phase 3 trial
candidates.one_line: Lecanemab, an antibody that clears amyloid from the brain, slowed decline on a dementia rating scale by about a quarter in a large phase 3 trial of early Alzheimer's disease. The FDA fully approved it in 2023.

candidates.title: One-time gene therapy keeps infants with severe spinal muscular atrophy alive
candidates.one_line: A single infusion of a working copy of the SMN1 gene let all 15 infants with the most severe spinal muscular atrophy survive past 20 months without permanent ventilation. The FDA approved it in 2019.

candidates.title: Gene therapy improves vision in inherited retinal disease and wins FDA approval
candidates.one_line: In a phase 3 trial, a one-time injection of a working RPE65 gene into the retina improved how well people with a rare inherited vision loss could move in dim light. The FDA approved it in 2017.

candidates.title: First CAR-T cell therapy approved for children with relapsed leukaemia
candidates.one_line: Tisagenlecleucel, made from a patient's own T cells re-engineered to attack leukaemia cells, put most children and young people with relapsed B-cell leukaemia into remission in a global trial. The FDA approved it in 2017.

candidates.title: First malaria vaccine RTS,S cuts clinical cases in African children
candidates.one_line: Final phase 3 results showed the RTS,S vaccine cut clinical malaria in African infants and children for years, more with a booster. Europe's regulator gave a positive opinion in 2015 and the WHO recommended it in 2021.

candidates.title: Base editing changes single DNA letters without cutting both strands
who: David Liu's lab at Harvard University and the Broad Institute
candidates.one_line: Liu's lab fused a disabled Cas9 to an enzyme that swaps one DNA letter for another. It corrected single-letter changes in cells without cutting both DNA strands.

candidates.title: Single-cell sequencing tracks development cell by cell in zebrafish, frog and flatworm
who: Harvard-based labs (Klein, Megason and Schier groups)
candidates.one_line: Several labs read the gene activity of tens of thousands of single cells in zebrafish and frog embryos and in flatworms, tracing how each cell type arises. Science named it the 2018 Breakthrough of the Year.

candidates.title: Two reviews find COVID-19 prediction and AI models unfit for clinical use
who: University of Cambridge team (Roberts et al.)
candidates.one_line: A living BMJ review of COVID-19 prediction models and a Nature Machine Intelligence review of imaging AI each found high risk of bias. Neither found a model ready for clinical use.

candidates.title: AlphaFold Database opens predicted structures for over 200 million proteins
candidates.one_line: DeepMind and EMBL-EBI released free AlphaFold 2 structure predictions for the human proteome and then, in 2022, for over 200 million proteins, which researchers worldwide now use daily.

candidates.title: First custom base-editing therapy treats an infant with a rare metabolic disease
candidates.one_line: Doctors built a base-editing therapy for one infant with a severe, rare urea-cycle disease in about six months and gave it in the clinic. The baby later improved. It is a proof of concept for custom gene editing.

candidates.title: AI tools design new proteins to order, tested in the lab
who: Baker lab, University of Washington Institute for Protein Design
candidates.one_line: Two Baker-lab deep-learning tools, ProteinMPNN and RFdiffusion, design protein shapes and sequences that did not exist in nature. Many of the designs folded and worked when made and tested in the lab.

candidates.title: RoseTTAFold predicts protein structures and complexes with a three-track network
who: Baker lab, University of Washington Institute for Protein Design
candidates.one_line: Months after AlphaFold 2, the Baker lab's RoseTTAFold, a smaller three-track neural network released openly, predicted protein structures and protein-protein complexes with comparable accuracy in many cases.

candidates.title: AlphaFold 3 predicts how proteins, DNA, RNA and drugs fit together
candidates.one_line: AlphaFold 3 predicts the joint structure of proteins with DNA, RNA, small-molecule drugs and ions, and beat other methods on several benchmarks. Its code was first withheld, then released for academic use.

candidates.title: AlphaMissense rates 71 million possible protein-changing DNA variants
candidates.one_line: DeepMind's AlphaMissense graded 71 million possible single-letter protein-changing variants as likely benign or likely harmful, and made the catalogue free to use. About 89 percent got a verdict.

candidates.title: First complete, gap-free sequence of a human genome published
candidates.one_line: The T2T consortium used long-read sequencing to assemble the first gap-free human genome, adding about 200 million letters, including centromeres and other hard regions missing from the old reference.

candidates.title: Complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly brain, neuron by neuron
candidates.one_line: A consortium mapped about 139,000 neurons and 50 million connections in an adult fruit fly brain, with machine-learning image segmentation and large-scale human proofreading, and released the map freely.

candidates.title: ECMWF runs its own AI weather model as a daily operational forecast
who: European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF)
candidates.one_line: On 25 February 2025 the European weather centre ECMWF began issuing forecasts from its own AI model, AIFS, as an operational product beside its physics-based forecast system.

candidates.title: GraphCast, an AI model, makes ten-day global forecasts in under a minute
candidates.one_line: Trained on about 40 years of weather records, GraphCast made a 10-day global forecast in under a minute and beat ECMWF's top deterministic system on 90 percent of 1,380 test measures.

candidates.title: Pangu-Weather, an AI model, forecasts global weather far faster than physics models
candidates.one_line: Huawei's Pangu-Weather, a 3D neural network trained on 39 years of weather records, forecast up to seven days ahead more accurately than ECMWF's operational system and about 10,000 times faster.

candidates.title: Ozone-damaging gas CFC-11 was being emitted again, partly from eastern China
who: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory and CIRES (University of Colorado Boulder)
University of Bristol and the AGAGE network (confirming study)
candidates.one_line: NOAA data showed the fall in the ozone-destroying gas CFC-11 had slowed by about half after 2012, which pointed to new emissions. A second network traced 40 to 60 percent of the rise to eastern China.

candidates.title: Antarctica's ice loss has tripled since 2012, a joint satellite assessment finds
who: IMBIE Team (led by Andrew Shepherd, University of Leeds, and Erik Ivins, NASA JPL)
candidates.one_line: Reconciling 24 satellite estimates, the IMBIE team found Antarctica lost about 2,720 billion tonnes of ice from 1992 to 2017, raising sea level by 7.6 millimetres, with the yearly loss tripling since 2012.

candidates.title: German reserves lost about 75 percent of flying-insect weight in 27 years
who: Radboud University and the Entomological Society Krefeld (Hallmann et al.)
Technical University of Munich and partners (Seibold et al., confirming study)
candidates.one_line: Traps in German reserves caught about 75 percent less flying-insect weight over 27 years. A larger German study of grasslands and forests later found falls in insect weight, numbers and species, while global trends are mixed.

candidates.title: InSight's marsquake recordings give the first measured look inside Mars
who: NASA InSight mission seismology teams (University of Cologne, ETH Zurich and partners)
candidates.one_line: Three papers used the InSight lander's marsquake recordings to measure Mars's crust, mantle and core. The core is liquid and about 1,830 kilometres in radius, larger than expected.

candidates.title: A 25-author assessment narrows how much warming doubled carbon dioxide brings
who: Sherwood et al., a 25-author World Climate Research Programme assessment team led from UNSW Sydney
candidates.one_line: Combining physics, the historical record and ancient climates, an assessment put the likely warming from doubled carbon dioxide at 2.6 to 3.9 degrees Celsius, tighter than the range used since 1979.

candidates.title: Samples from asteroid Ryugu match rare water-rich meteorites and carry organics
who: JAXA Hayabusa2 project and its initial-analysis teams (including Tohoku University)
candidates.one_line: Samples returned by Japan's Hayabusa2 in December 2020 match rare, water-rich CI-type meteorites and carry organic molecules, giving an uncontaminated look at early solar system material.

candidates.title: Deep learning identifies and counts wild animals in camera-trap photos
ai_systems: Deep convolutional neural networks trained on Snapshot Serengeti images (University of Wyoming and partners)
who: University of Wyoming (Norouzzadeh, Clune) and the Snapshot Serengeti project (University of Minnesota, Oxford and partners)
candidates.one_line: Neural networks trained on 3.2 million Serengeti camera-trap images named species with about 96.6 percent accuracy, matching volunteers and saving more than 8 years of human labelling.

candidates.title: Bennu samples hold ammonia, amino acids, all five nucleobases and brine salts
who: NASA OSIRIS-REx sample analysis teams (NASA Goddard; Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History and partners)
candidates.one_line: Samples from asteroid Bennu, returned in September 2023, hold ammonia, amino acids, all five nucleobases and salts left by ancient brine, showing watery chemistry and life's ingredients on a small body.

candidates.title: The Antarctic ozone hole starts to shrink after the ban on CFCs
who: Massachusetts Institute of Technology and partners (Solomon et al.)
candidates.one_line: A fingerprint study of September ozone data found the Antarctic ozone hole shrinking since 2000, by about 4.5 million square kilometres, as chlorine from banned CFCs declines.

candidates.title: AI reading ship tracks maps where the world's fishing fleet works
ai_systems: Convolutional neural networks on vessel tracks (Global Fishing Watch)
who: Global Fishing Watch, Google, SkyTruth and Oceana, with the University of California Santa Barbara and Dalhousie University
candidates.one_line: Neural networks trained on 22 billion ship-position messages sorted out fishing from other vessel movement and showed that fishing covers at least 55 percent of the world's ocean area.

candidates.title: Hunga Tonga's 2022 eruption sent pressure waves around the world several times
who: University of California Santa Barbara-led international team (Matoza et al.)
University of Bath-led international team (Wright et al.)
candidates.one_line: After the January 2022 Hunga Tonga eruption, barometers, seismometers and satellites recorded pressure waves that travelled around the planet several times and rose to the edge of space.

candidates.title: New Horizons gives the first close look at Pluto and its moons
who: NASA New Horizons team (Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory and Southwest Research Institute)
candidates.one_line: NASA's New Horizons flew past Pluto on 14 July 2015 and showed mountains of water ice, a young nitrogen-ice plain, thin hazy air and active geology on a world once thought dead.

candidates.title: GenCast, an AI model, makes 15-day probabilistic forecasts in minutes
candidates.one_line: GenCast, a diffusion-based AI ensemble from Google DeepMind, made 15-day probabilistic global forecasts in about eight minutes and beat ECMWF's ensemble on 97 percent of 1,320 test measures.

candidates.title: Replication of 100 psychology studies finds weaker effects than the originals
candidates.one_line: A team of about 270 researchers repeated 100 psychology studies. Of the originals, 97 reported significant results; 36 of the repeats did. Average effect sizes fell by about half.

candidates.title: 29 teams analyse one dataset and reach different answers
who: 29 analyst teams coordinated by Raphael Silberzahn and Eric L. Uhlmann
Center for Open Science (Brian Nosek, co-author)
candidates.one_line: Twenty-nine teams analysed one soccer dataset to ask whether referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players. Odds ratios ran from 0.89 to 2.93, and nine teams found no significant effect.

candidates.title: Language models can imitate survey respondents from different groups
who: Brigham Young University (Lisa Argyle, Ethan Busby, Joshua Gubler, David Wingate and colleagues)
candidates.one_line: Researchers prompted GPT-3 with the backstories of real US survey respondents. The authors say its answers matched patterns of voting and opinion in survey data closely enough to stand in for some human samples.

candidates.title: A nudge meta-analysis is challenged: the effect may vanish after bias correction
who: University of Geneva (Stephanie Mertens, Tobias Brosch and colleagues)
University College London and University of Amsterdam (Maximilian Maier and colleagues)
ELTE Eotvos Lorand University (Barnabas Szaszi and colleagues)
candidates.one_line: A meta-analysis of hundreds of nudge studies found a medium average effect. Two letters in the same journal said the evidence for nudging is weak or absent once publication bias is corrected.

candidates.title: History database tests moralizing gods, then a dispute over missing data
who: Seshat: Global History Databank (Harvey Whitehouse, Peter Turchin, Pieter Francois and colleagues)
candidates.one_line: A Nature study using the Seshat historical databank found that large, complex societies came before gods who police morals. A 2021 reply said the way missing data were treated drove that conclusion.

candidates.title: 2020 election feed experiments find little change in political attitudes
who: US 2020 Facebook and Instagram Election Study academic team (Talia Stroud, Joshua Tucker and colleagues)
candidates.one_line: Experiments on Facebook and Instagram in the 2020 US election swapped algorithmic feeds for chronological ones, cut reshares and reduced like-minded sources. None detectably changed users' political attitudes in the study period.

candidates.title: Aid bundle for the very poor raises incomes in six countries
who: Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo, Dean Karlan, Christopher Udry and colleagues
Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL)
candidates.one_line: Trials in six countries found that giving very poor households an asset, training, coaching and savings raised their consumption and income, and gains lasted a year after the programme ended.

candidates.title: Housing voucher counselling moves families to high-opportunity neighbourhoods
who: Opportunity Insights at Harvard University (Peter Bergman, Raj Chetty, Stefanie DeLuca, Nathaniel Hendren, Lawrence Katz, Christopher Palmer)
Seattle Housing Authority and King County Housing Authority
candidates.one_line: A randomised trial in the Seattle area found that tailored help with housing searches and landlords moved voucher families into high-opportunity neighbourhoods at about 53 percent, against about 15 percent without the help.

candidates.title: A fine-tuned language model predicts human choices across psychology experiments
who: Helmholtz Munich (Marcel Binz, Eric Schulz and colleagues)
candidates.one_line: A language model fine-tuned on choices from a large set of psychology experiments predicted human choices in new tasks better than existing cognitive models. Critics said it may not capture human cognition.

candidates.title: Machine-learning ink detection lets contestants read sealed Herculaneum scrolls
ai_systems: machine-learning ink-detection models written by Vesuvius Challenge contestants (convolutional neural networks trained on scan data)
who: Youssef Nader, Luke Farritor and Julian Schilliger (Grand Prize team)
EduceLab, University of Kentucky (W. Brent Seales)
candidates.one_line: Contestants used machine-learning ink detection on X-ray scans to read the first words, then over 2,000 characters, of a carbonised Greek scroll from Herculaneum that stayed sealed since the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79.

candidates.title: Ancient DNA shows steppe herders reshaped Europe's ancestry about 4,500 years ago
who: Wolfgang Haak, Johannes Krause, David Reich and colleagues
Morten Allentoft, Eske Willerslev and colleagues, University of Copenhagen
candidates.one_line: Two groups sequenced Bronze Age skeletons from across Eurasia and found a large migration of steppe herders into Europe, which changed its ancestry and may have carried Indo-European languages.

candidates.title: Ithaca neural network restores, places and dates damaged Greek inscriptions
who: Ca' Foscari University of Venice (Thea Sommerschield)
Athens University of Economics and Business (John Pavlopoulos, Ion Androutsopoulos)
candidates.one_line: A deep neural network trained on Greek inscriptions restores missing text, suggests where an inscription was made and dates it; historians using it restored damaged text much more accurately than without it.

candidates.title: Footprints at White Sands dated to about 23,000 years ago
who: Matthew Bennett (Bournemouth University), David Bustos (US National Park Service) and Jeffrey Pigati (US Geological Survey) with colleagues
candidates.one_line: Human footprints in lake-edge sediments at White Sands, New Mexico, were dated to 21,000 to 23,000 years ago, placing people in North America at the height of the last ice age; later dating by other methods agreed.

candidates.title: Laser mapping reveals 60,000 hidden Maya structures in northern Guatemala
who: Marcello Canuto, Francisco Estrada-Belli and colleagues, Tulane University, with the PACUNAM LiDAR Initiative (Guatemala)
candidates.one_line: Airborne laser scanning of about 2,100 square kilometres of forest in Guatemala found more than 60,000 hidden Maya houses, fortifications, roads and canals, showing a denser and more connected lowland society than thought.

candidates.title: Jebel Irhoud fossils put early Homo sapiens at about 300,000 years ago
who: Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology (Jean-Jacques Hublin, Daniel Richter)
National Institute of Archaeology and Heritage, Morocco
candidates.one_line: New skull and face fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, re-dated to about 315,000 years ago, put the first Homo sapiens roughly 100,000 years earlier than the oldest earlier finds and across Africa.

candidates.title: Homo naledi: a new small-brained human species from South Africa
who: Lee Berger and the Rising Star Expedition team, University of the Witwatersrand
candidates.one_line: More than 1,500 bone fragments from at least 15 individuals in a deep cave chamber defined Homo naledi, a small-brained human species with a body that mixes primitive and modern features.

candidates.title: Aeneas network finds parallels, restores and dates Latin inscriptions
who: Ca' Foscari University of Venice (Thea Sommerschield)
candidates.one_line: A generative neural network takes a Latin inscription's text and image, retrieves similar inscriptions, restores gaps of unknown length and suggests a date and province; historians tested it on real stones.

candidates.title: Denisovan jawbone found on the Tibetan plateau, far from Siberia
who: Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology (Jean-Jacques Hublin, Frido Welker)
candidates.one_line: A jawbone at least 160,000 years old from Baishiya Karst Cave in Tibet was identified as Denisovan from its ancient proteins, the first Denisovan fossil known outside Denisova Cave in Siberia.

candidates.title: Deep learning helps find 303 new Nazca geoglyph figures
ai_systems: deep-learning image classifier for aerial photographs (Yamagata University and IBM Research)
candidates.one_line: A deep-learning model screened aerial images of the Nazca plain in Peru and, after field checks, 303 new figure-type geoglyphs were confirmed, almost doubling the number of known figures.

candidates.title: Virtual unwrapping reads a burned 1,700-year-old Hebrew scroll unopened
who: University of Kentucky (W. Brent Seales, Clifford Seth Parker)
Hebrew University of Jerusalem (Michael Segal, Emanuel Tov)
candidates.one_line: Scanning and software flattened a charred scroll from the En-Gedi synagogue without opening it, and its first chapters of Leviticus read the same as the standard Hebrew text, the oldest such book text found in a synagogue.

candidates.title: Aguada Fenix: the oldest and largest known Maya monument
who: University of Arizona (Takeshi Inomata, Daniela Triadan)
candidates.one_line: Laser mapping and excavation at Aguada Fenix, Mexico, revealed a raised platform about 1.4 kilometres long built around 1000 to 800 BCE, the largest and oldest Maya monument known.

candidates.title: Laser survey finds 2,000-year-old urban settlements in the Ecuadorian Amazon
who: French National Centre for Scientific Research (Stephen Rostain and colleagues)
candidates.one_line: Laser mapping and excavation in the Upano Valley, Ecuador, revealed thousands of earthen platforms, plazas and roads of a society that lived in dense settlements from about 500 BCE to 600 CE.

candidates.title: Linear Elamite, a 4,000-year-old Iranian script, is deciphered
who: French National Centre for Scientific Research (Francois Desset) with Kambiz Tabibzadeh, Matthieu Kervran, Gian Pietro Basello and Gianni Marchesi
candidates.one_line: A team proposed readings for nearly all signs of Linear Elamite, a script of about 2300 BCE from south-western Iran, and read many of its inscriptions for the first time.

candidates.title: Handwriting analysis finds many writers in Judah's Arad letters, about 600 BCE
ai_systems: handwriting-analysis algorithms for ancient ink inscriptions (Tel Aviv University team; no product name)
who: Tel Aviv University (Shira Faigenbaum-Golovin, Arie Shaus, Barak Sober, Eli Piasetzky, Israel Finkelstein and colleagues)
candidates.one_line: Handwriting-analysis software applied to 16 ink inscriptions from the Judahite fortress of Arad found at least six writers, suggesting wide literacy in Judah shortly before the Babylonian conquest and bearing on when biblical books were written.

candidates.title: Neural network translates Akkadian cuneiform texts into English
ai_systems: neural machine translation model for Akkadian (Open University of Israel and Tel Aviv University team)
who: Tel Aviv University (Omer Levy, Jonathan Berant)
candidates.one_line: A neural model translated Akkadian, the language of ancient Mesopotamia, into English from transliterations and, less well, from cuneiform signs, with output scored against human translations.

candidates.title: AI handwriting model dates Dead Sea Scrolls, some older than expected
ai_systems: Enoch (handwriting-based dating model, University of Groningen)
who: University of Groningen (Mladen Popovic, Maruf Dhali, Lambert Schomaker)
candidates.one_line: A handwriting model calibrated on radiocarbon-dated Dead Sea Scrolls estimated dates for undated manuscripts and suggested that some are older than scholars' handwriting-based dates.

candidates.title: Meta's MMS speech models cover over 1,100 languages using Bible recordings
who: Meta AI (Vineel Pratap, Michael Auli and colleagues)
candidates.one_line: Meta released speech recognition and speech generation models for over 1,100 languages, trained largely on labelled recordings of Bible readings, widening language-documentation tools to small languages.
